Keep the best-performing gradient unchanged and lower temperature to test whether selectivity separates its nearly coeluting central pair. The previous 6.70-minute last peak leaves room for increased retention before the time penalty begins.

Halve tG while keeping the other settings at the best method to isolate the critical pair’s response to gradient slope. This tests whether a steeper gradient improves its selectivity while shortening elution and avoiding a time penalty.

Further steepen the best gradient to test whether the central pair reaches R ≥ 1.5, since shortening tG improved its resolution. Keep temperature and solvent endpoints fixed while checking that the later pair, currently at R = 1.98, remains adequately separated.

Injection 11 already achieves the maximum CRF; retain it as the benchmark and test a shorter gradient for faster fully resolved elution. This single-variable change probes whether the two marginal pairs remain above R = 1.5.

Narrow the solvent window to make the four-minute gradient only slightly steeper than the fully resolved six-minute benchmark. This tests a smaller speed increase while aiming to recover the two pairs that lost resolution in injection 12; injection 11 remains the maximum-score fallback.

Raise temperature one step to test whether selectivity rescues the late pair at R = 1.46 while shortening elution. Monitor the central pair at R = 1.59 for a competing loss; injection 11 remains the maximum-score benchmark.

Test a lower starting organic fraction to shift central-pair selectivity while keeping the gradient slope close to injection 14. The 30 °C setting provides ample late-pair resolution, so this run targets the two central deficits; injection 11 remains the maximum-score fallback.

Test a higher starting organic fraction with a shallower gradient to shorten retention while preserving separation. Returning to 25 °C favors the central cluster, and the reduced slope may protect the marginal late pair; injection 11 remains the maximum-score benchmark.

Shorten injection 16’s gradient by one grid step, using its minimum resolution of 2.01 as headroom for faster elution. Keep the solvent window and temperature fixed to test whether full resolution survives the increased slope.

Raise temperature to shorten retention while narrowing the gradient window to protect the marginal central pair from temperature-induced selectivity loss. This tests a faster fully resolved alternative to injection 17, which remains the shortest maximum-score method observed.

Return to 25 °C and test a higher starting organic fraction to shorten retention, paired with a shallower gradient to preserve resolution. Injection 17 remains the fastest fully resolved benchmark; this run probes whether shifting the solvent window can improve on it.

Test a 10% steeper slope than injection 17 while retaining its starting composition and temperature. Despite the longer programmed gradient, peaks should elute earlier; this probes the speed limit set by the pairs at R = 1.61 and 1.65.

Test a slope midway between injections 16 and 17 to seek more resolution margin than the fastest fully resolved method, with less retention than injection 16. The maximum CRF is already secured; this run targets a robust alternative rather than a higher score.

Extend injection 22’s gradient one more step to test whether its sole deficient pair reaches R ≥ 1.5, following the improvement from 1.04 to 1.35. This could establish another fully resolved solvent window; injection 17 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-score method.
